title: Block 3 Practice Test 1
context: Foundations of Medicine, Block 3, Weeks 9 to 12

questions.p:
Which of the following are associated with target cells on the blood film?
i) Liver disease
ii) Hyposplenism
iii) Thalassemia
iv) Hereditary spherocytosis
questions.e:
Correct: C. Target cells come from excess membrane relative to cell volume. Causes include liver disease and alcohol, hyposplenism, thalassemia, and rarely severe iron deficiency.
A: Hereditary spherocytosis gives spherocytes, not target cells.
B: This leaves out hyposplenism.
D: Statement iv) gives spherocytes.
Takeaway: Spherocytes: hereditary spherocytosis and autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

questions.p: Victor, 55, has a lymphoma found only in his stomach. CT shows no enlarged lymph nodes and his marrow is clear. He has no fever, night sweats or weight loss. What is his Ann Arbor stage?
questions.e:
Correct: A. A single extralymphatic organ or site with no nodes is stage IE. No B symptoms gives the A suffix.
B: B needs B symptoms.
C: Stage IV is diffuse extralymphatic involvement, such as marrow.
D: Stage II needs two or more node regions, or an extralymphatic site with nodes, on one side of the diaphragm.
Takeaway: Stage I: one region or one extralymphatic site.

questions.p: A man with a ruptured spleen is in a massive transfusion and needs replacement of all his clotting factors. The product is stored in a freezer and must be thawed before use. Which product is it?
questions.e:
Correct: B. Plasma contains all coagulation factors. It is stored at -18°C for up to 1 year and takes about 20 minutes to thaw.
A: Platelets are stored at room temperature for up to 7 days, as in your Week 10 quiz.
C: Fibrinogen concentrate replaces fibrinogen only.
D: Cryoprecipitate is also frozen, but it holds FVIII, FXIII, vWF and fibrinogen, not all factors.
E: PCC holds the vitamin K dependent factors.
Takeaway: Room temperature: platelets and fibrinogen concentrate. Fridge: red cells. Freezer: plasma and cryo.

questions.p: In a trial, a new drug lowers the relapse rate from 20% in the control group to 15% in the treatment group. What are the absolute risk reduction and the number needed to treat?
questions.e:
Correct: D. ARR is control risk minus treatment risk: 20% minus 15% is 5%. NNT is the number treated to prevent one event: 1 divided by 0.05 is 20.
A: 25% is the relative risk reduction (5 divided by 20), not the ARR.
B: NNT is 1 divided by 0.05, which is 20.
C: 15% is the risk in the treatment group.
Takeaway: NNT = 1 / ARR.

questions.p: Which pairing of antiplatelet drug and its target is correct?
questions.e:
Correct: A. Clopidogrel blocks the P2Y12 receptor pathway, which ADP from the dense granules acts on.
B: Abciximab is directed against glycoprotein IIb/IIIa.
C: Aspirin inhibits cyclooxygenase and lowers thromboxane A2.
D: Clopidogrel acts on P2Y12, and aspirin is the drug that lowers thromboxane A2.
Takeaway: Aspirin: COX. Clopidogrel: P2Y12. Abciximab: GPIIb/IIIa.

questions.p: Sophie, 24, has classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Staging shows stage IIA disease with a bulky mediastinal mass. Which treatment plan fits best?
o: A full course, ABVD × 2 then AVD × 4
Watch and wait until B symptoms appear
A short course of chemotherapy, then radiation
questions.e:
Correct: B. Bulky disease is often treated like advanced stage. She gets the full course of ABVD × 2 then AVD × 4, with radiation if a PET-positive residual mass persists.
A: Chemotherapy is the main modality in Hodgkin lymphoma.
C: All Hodgkin patients are treated, aiming to cure.
D: A short course then involved-field radiation is for non-bulky stage I to II.
Takeaway: Bulky early stage Hodgkin is treated as advanced.

questions.p: Which test result is high in anemia of chronic inflammation but low in iron deficiency anemia?
questions.e:
Correct: C. In anemia of chronic inflammation, hepcidin traps iron in stores, so ferritin is high. In iron deficiency, stores are empty, so ferritin is low.
A: RDW is high in iron deficiency.
B: Transferrin is high in iron deficiency and low in chronic inflammation.
D: Serum transferrin receptor is high in iron deficiency.
Takeaway: Ferritin reflects body iron stores.

questions.p: Which hereditary hemolytic anemia is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern?
questions.e:
Correct: D. G6PD deficiency is X-linked recessive and common in Africans, Asians and Mediterraneans.
A: β-thalassemia major is a homozygous globin gene defect, not X-linked.
B: Sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive.
C: Hereditary spherocytosis is autosomal dominant.
Takeaway: Hemolysis labs: high retics, LDH and indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin.

questions.p: Which imaging test is the standard of care for bony disease in multiple myeloma?
questions.e:
Correct: D. Lytic lesions or fractures can show on XR, CT, PET-CT or MRI, and the skeletal survey is the standard of care.
A: A bone scan is listed for lymphoma bone involvement.
B: The free light chain assay finds the M protein, not bone lesions.
C: Flow cytometry studies the marrow plasma cells.
Takeaway: Myeloma bone disease: skeletal survey.

questions.p: Smudge cells on the peripheral blood film are associated with which disorder?
questions.e:
Correct: C. Smudge cells on the film are a feature of CLL, a clonal malignancy of mature B cells.
A: CML shows a bimodal spread of myelocytes and neutrophils.
B: ALL shows blasts with no granules.
D: Myelofibrosis shows teardrop cells.
Takeaway: CLL is the most common leukemia, with a median age of 70.

questions.p:
Which are palliative uses of radiation therapy?
i) Spinal cord compression
ii) Superior vena cava syndrome
iii) Bleeding from a GI or gynecologic tumour
iv) CNS prophylaxis in ALL
questions.e:
Correct: B. Cord compression, vascular compression such as SVC syndrome and tumour bleeding are listed palliative uses.
A: This leaves out tumour bleeding.
C: CNS prophylaxis in ALL is a curative use.
D: Statement iv) is a curative use.
Takeaway: Radiation cures limited disease and palliates compression and bleeding.

questions.p:
Hana, 16, has had heavy periods since menarche that soak through a pad every hour. She has had nosebleeds since childhood that needed cautery, and she bled for 2 days after a tooth extraction. Her mother bruises easily and had a postpartum hemorrhage. She takes no drugs. Exam shows scattered bruises on her shins.

Hb 106 g/L (ref 115-160)
MCV 76 fL (ref 80-100)
Platelets 240 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
PT/INR normal
aPTT mildly prolonged
vWF antigen low
vWF activity low, in proportion to antigen

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. Mucosal bleeding in a girl, an affected mother, a normal platelet count, and a proportional drop in vWF antigen and activity fit type 1 VWD, the most common form. Inheritance is autosomal, so both sexes are affected.
A: Hemophilia A is X-linked, mostly affects males, and causes joint and muscle bleeds.
B: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is a platelet aggregation disorder, with normal vWF levels.
C: Type 2 is qualitative, with vWF activity under 70% of the antigen.
D: ITP gives a low platelet count.
Takeaway: Treat type 1 VWD with DDAVP, and tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeding.

questions.p: Which describes standard treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia?
o: 2-3 years of chemotherapy with CNS prophylaxis
A tyrosine kinase inhibitor taken daily for life
Surgery and radiation as the main curative tools
7+3 induction, with treatment over in 4-6 months
questions.e:
Correct: A. ALL treatment runs 2 to 3 years on the Dana-Farber protocol: induction, consolidation and low-dose maintenance, plus CNS prophylaxis by LP or radiation. About 90% of children are cured.
B: A daily TKI is chronic treatment for CML.
C: Radiation and surgery are not treatment options for acute leukemia.
D: 7+3 induction over 4 to 6 months is the AML timeline.
Takeaway: Children with ALL: 90% cured.

questions.p:
Rosa, 31, has systemic lupus erythematosus. Over 2 weeks she has grown tired and short of breath, and her family noticed her eyes are yellow. She has no new drugs, no fever and no recent infection. On exam she is pale and jaundiced, with a palpable spleen tip.

Hb 78 g/L (ref 115-160)
MCV 104 fL (ref 80-100)
Reticulocytes high
WBC 6.0 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 210 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
LDH high
Indirect bilirubin high
Haptoglobin low
DAT positive for IgG
Film: spherocytes and polychromasia. No agglutination.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. Hemolysis labs, spherocytes and a positive DAT for IgG in a patient with SLE fit warm AIHA. The antibodies bind at 37°C, and SLE is a listed cause. The raised MCV comes from the reticulocytosis.
A: Hereditary spherocytosis has a negative DAT.
B: Cold AIHA is IgM with C3 on the DAT, and shows agglutination.
C: TTP has schistocytes and severe thrombocytopenia.
D: G6PD deficiency has a negative DAT, with bite cells.
Takeaway: Warm AIHA: steroids if severe, splenectomy, immunosuppressive drugs.

questions.p: A patient on hemodialysis for kidney failure has a new proximal DVT. Which anticoagulant fits best?
questions.e:
Correct: C. Warfarin is the listed DVT treatment for patients with renal failure. LMWH, fondaparinux and the direct Xa inhibitors are cleared by the kidney, and their half-life lengthens in renal failure.
A: Dalteparin is renally cleared, and its half-life lengthens in renal failure.
B: Fondaparinux is renally cleared.
D: Rivaroxaban is renally cleared.
Takeaway: LMWH for cancer and pregnancy. Warfarin for renal failure.

questions.p: A 70-year-old man arrives in hemorrhagic shock after a crash. His blood group is unknown and red cells are needed before testing can be done. Which group should the blood bank issue?
questions.e:
Correct: B. O negative is the universal red cell donor, but O positive is used for males and for women over 45. O negative is kept for women under 45.
A: O negative is kept for women under 45.
C: AB negative is not a universal donor group.
D: AB positive is the universal recipient, not the universal donor.
Takeaway: Red cells: O donor, AB recipient. Plasma: AB donor.

questions.p: Which set of lab changes fits tumour lysis syndrome?
o: High K, high phosphate, high uric acid, low calcium
Low K, high phosphate, low uric acid, high calcium
Low K, low phosphate, low uric acid, low calcium
High K, low phosphate, high uric acid, high calcium
questions.e:
Correct: A. Tumour lysis syndrome brings hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia and acidosis, which can lead to acute renal failure.
B: Potassium and uric acid rise, and calcium falls.
C: Potassium, phosphate and uric acid all rise.
D: Phosphate rises and calcium falls.
Takeaway: Prevent it with hydration and allopurinol or rasburicase.

questions.p:
Gordon, 64, is on day 7 of unfractionated heparin prophylaxis after hip replacement. He now has a swollen, painful left calf, and ultrasound shows a new DVT. He has no bleeding. He has no other new drugs, and his blood cultures are negative.

Hb 118 g/L (ref 135-170)
WBC 8.2 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 92 (was 260 before surgery) × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
PT/INR normal
Fibrinogen normal
Film: no schistocytes.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. A platelet fall of more than half, 5 to 10 days into heparin, with a new thrombosis and no bleeding, fits HIT. Antibodies form against the heparin-PF4 complex and activate platelets.
A: TTP shows schistocytes and hemolytic anemia.
B: Dilution follows massive transfusion and does not cause a new clot.
C: DIC raises the INR and lowers fibrinogen.
D: ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion and does not cause thrombosis on heparin.
Takeaway: HIT: stop all heparin, start a non-heparin anticoagulant, avoid platelet transfusions.

questions.p: Which test in the von Willebrand disease screen measures vWF quality?
questions.e:
Correct: D. The VWD screen has three parts: vWF antigen for quantity, vWF activity for quality, and factor VIII activity for the carrier role.
A: Factor VIII activity assesses vWF's role as a protective carrier.
B: vWF antigen measures quantity.
C: The platelet count can be low in type 2B but does not measure vWF.
Takeaway: Type 2 VWD: vWF activity is under 70% of the vWF antigen.

questions.p:
Dennis, 52, has had headaches and itchy skin after every hot shower for months. His toes burn and turn red at times. He does not smoke, has no lung or heart disease, and does not snore. On exam he has a ruddy face and a palpable spleen.

Hb 188 g/L (ref 135-170)
Hematocrit 0.56
WBC 13.2 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 520 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Serum EPO low
JAK2 V617F positive

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. Erythrocytosis with aquagenic pruritus, erythromelalgia, a ruddy face, splenomegaly, a low EPO and JAK2 V617F fit polycythemia vera. When Hb, platelets and WBC are all high, treat it as erythrocytosis.
A: An EPO-secreting tumour raises EPO.
B: Secondary erythrocytosis has a normal or high EPO, and he has no hypoxic cause.
C: ET mainly raises platelets, without erythrocytosis.
D: CML gives a very high WBC with basophilia, not a high Hb.
Takeaway: PV: ASA 81 mg plus hematocrit under 0.45.

questions.p: Which of the following is a minor WHO criterion for polycythemia vera?
o: A platelet count of 450 or more
questions.e:
Correct: D. Polycythemia vera has one minor WHO criterion: a subnormal serum EPO. The major criteria are a high Hb or hematocrit, a hypercellular marrow, and a JAK2 mutation.
A: A high EPO points to secondary erythrocytosis.
B: Palpable splenomegaly is a minor criterion for primary myelofibrosis.
C: A platelet count of 450 or more is the first major criterion for ET.
Takeaway: Low EPO is primary. Normal or high EPO is secondary.

questions.p: In febrile neutropenia, when should IV vancomycin be added to empiric antibiotics?
o: Only if the fever lasts more than 72 hours
Skin or catheter infection, or instability
Every patient, as part of the first dose
Only once blood cultures grow a gram-positive
questions.e:
Correct: B. Start broad-spectrum antibiotics such as IV piperacillin-tazobactam or imipenem. Add IV vancomycin if there are signs of skin or IV catheter site infection, or the patient is hemodynamically unstable.
A: No fever-duration rule is given for adding vancomycin.
C: Vancomycin is added only for those indications, not for everyone.
D: Empiric treatment does not wait for culture results.
Takeaway: Febrile neutropenia is an oncologic emergency.

questions.p:
Noah, 5, has 3 weeks of tiredness, pale skin, nosebleeds and bone pain that wakes him at night. He has had two fevers. On exam he has pallor, bruises, enlarged nodes in the neck and an enlarged liver and spleen. Chest X-ray shows a mediastinal mass.

Hb 72 g/L (ref 110-140)
WBC 48 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 31 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
LDH high
Uric acid high
Film: many blasts with no granules.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: C. A child with marrow failure, bone pain, organ enlargement, a mediastinal mass and blasts without granules has ALL. ALL makes up 80% of childhood leukemias.
A: AML is 15% of childhood leukemias, and its blasts often carry an Auer rod.
B: Aplastic anemia has no blasts and no organ enlargement.
D: CML is rare in children and shows mature myeloid cells.
E: ITP lowers platelets only.
Takeaway: About 90% of children with ALL are cured.

questions.p: Patient A, 47, has bleeding gums and petechiae. Her platelets are 12, and INR, PTT and fibrinogen are normal. Patient B, 47, has a swollen, painful knee from a bleed into the joint. His PTT is prolonged and his CBC is normal. Which type of hemostatic problem does each have, in order?
questions.e:
Correct: A. Mucosal bleeding with a low platelet count is a primary hemostatic problem. Deep bleeding with a prolonged PTT is a secondary problem.
B: Patient A has severe thrombocytopenia, which is primary.
C: This reverses the two patterns.
D: Patient B has a prolonged PTT and a normal platelet count, which is secondary.
Takeaway: Mucosal bleeding is more likely primary. Deep bleeding is more likely secondary.

questions.p: Which platelet function disorder is a disorder of platelet aggregation?
questions.e:
Correct: C. Glanzmann thrombasthenia is the listed disorder of platelet aggregation.
A: Scott syndrome is a disorder of pro-coagulant activity.
B: Gray platelet syndrome is a disorder of granules.
D: Bernard Soulier syndrome is a disorder of adhesion.
Takeaway: Platelet function disorders give mucosal bleeding and easy bruising.

questions.p: Which statement about bone marrow sampling is correct?
o: Sternal aspirates are allowed, sternal cores are not
The tibia is an accepted aspirate site in adults
The PSIS is reserved for children and avoided in adults
Core biopsies may be taken from the ribs
questions.e:
Correct: A. The PSIS is the standard site. In extenuating circumstances the sternum can be used for an aspirate, but a core biopsy is never taken from the sternum because it is too close to the heart.
B: The tibia is used only in children.
C: The PSIS is the standard site in adults and children, as in your Week 11 quiz.
D: Core biopsies are never taken from the ribs.
Takeaway: Core biopsy: never sternum, tibia, skull or ribs.

questions.p:
Clifford, 72, has 4 months of back pain, fatigue and thirst. He has had two chest infections this year. He is confused today. X-rays show lytic lesions in his spine and skull.

Hb 88 g/L (ref 135-170)
MCV 92 fL (ref 80-100)
WBC 4.1 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 168 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Calcium 2.98 mmol/L
Creatinine 210 µmol/L
Albumin low
Total protein high
Film: rouleaux.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. He meets the CRAB criteria: calcium over 2.52, creatinine over 175, Hb under 100 and lytic bone lesions. With rouleaux and recurrent infections, this is multiple myeloma.
A: MGUS causes no organ damage.
B: CLL raises lymphocytes and shows smudge cells.
C: A solitary plasmacytoma is a single tumour without widespread organ damage.
D: Nothing points to a prostate primary, and it would not explain the rouleaux.
Takeaway: Confirm with protein electrophoresis, free light chains and a marrow biopsy.

questions.p:
Sofia, 24, of Greek descent, is seen for fatigue before a planned pregnancy. She has normal periods, eats a varied diet including red meat, and has never had a GI bleed. Her mother was told she had "small blood cells" years ago. On exam she has mild pallor, no jaundice and no splenomegaly.

Hb 108 g/L (ref 115-160)
MCV 62 fL (ref 80-100)
RBC count high
RDW normal
WBC 6.2 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 260 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Ferritin normal
HbA2 elevated
Film: hypochromic microcytes with target cells.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: D. A Mediterranean woman with a very low MCV, a high RBC count, a normal ferritin, a family history and a raised HbA2 has β-thalassemia minor, the heterozygous form.
A: Anemia of chronic inflammation needs a significant other medical problem, and she has none.
B: Iron deficiency gives a low ferritin and a high RDW.
C: Sideroblastic anemia needs a toxin, drug, B6 deficiency or MDS, and shows basophilic stippling.
E: α-thalassemia is more common in Southeast Asia and Africa and has a normal HbA2.
Takeaway: Thalassemia: high RBC count. Iron deficiency: low RBC count, high RDW.

questions.p:
Dennis, 68, has 3 months of fatigue and shortness of breath on stairs. He has had black stools on and off and takes ibuprofen daily for knee pain. He craves ice. On exam he is pale, with a resting heart rate of 104 and spoon-shaped nails.

Hb 82 g/L (ref 135-170)
MCV 68 fL (ref 80-100)
RDW high
WBC 7.1 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 480 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Ferritin low
Transferrin high
Film: hypochromic microcytes with anisocytosis, poikilocytosis and elliptocytes.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: B. Melena on daily ibuprofen, pica, koilonychia, a low ferritin, a high transferrin and a high RDW point to iron deficiency from GI blood loss. Iron deficiency is also a listed cause of reactive thrombocytosis.
A: Lead poisoning shows basophilic stippling.
C: Anemia of chronic inflammation has a high ferritin and low transferrin.
D: β-thalassemia minor has a normal ferritin and a raised HbA2.
E: Sideroblastic anemia has normal iron stores and basophilic stippling.
Takeaway: In iron deficiency, find the source of loss. In an older man, think GI bleeding.

questions.p: Which of the following is associated with t(15;17)?
questions.e:
Correct: E. t(15;17), giving the PML/RARα fusion gene, confirms acute promyelocytic leukemia.
A: Myeloma FISH looks for t(4;14), t(14;16) and del(17p).
B: CLL is tested with FISH but has no listed translocation.
C: CML has t(9;22), the Philadelphia chromosome.
D: Follicular lymphoma has t(14;18).
Takeaway: APL is treated with ATRA and arsenic.

questions.p: Which anemia is treated with erythropoietin in severe cases?
o: Iron deficiency anemia from blood loss
questions.e:
Correct: B. Anemia of chronic inflammation is treated by targeting the underlying disease, and erythropoietin is used in severe cases.
A: β-thalassemia minor is mild and needs genetic counselling, not EPO.
C: Iron deficiency is treated with iron replacement.
D: Hereditary spherocytosis is treated with folate, vaccination and penicillin prophylaxis.
Takeaway: Anemia of chronic inflammation seldom needs a transfusion.

questions.p: Vincristine is the O in CHOP-R. Which statement about how it works is correct?
o: It inhibits microtubule assembly in M phase
It interferes with nucleic acid metabolism
It cross-links guanine and blocks S phase entry
It inhibits topoisomerase II and intercalates DNA
questions.e:
Correct: A. Vincristine (Oncovin) is a vinca alkaloid. It inhibits microtubule assembly in metaphase and disrupts M phase.
B: Interfering with nucleic acid metabolism describes anti-metabolites such as methotrexate.
C: Cross-linking guanine describes alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide.
D: Topoisomerase II inhibition and intercalation describe anti-tumour antibiotics such as doxorubicin.
Takeaway: Know one mechanism per class.

questions.p: Investigators compare a new oral drug with the standard IV drug. They expect it to work about as well, but it is easier to take and less toxic. Which trial design fits?
questions.e:
Correct: D. A non-inferiority trial shows that the new therapy is not clinically worse than the comparator. It suits a drug that may not work better but offers safety, tolerability or convenience.
A: An equivalence trial shows the difference lies between a lower and an upper margin.
B: Phase 1 trials study safety and dose in 10 to 30 people.
C: A superiority trial expects the new drug to work better.
Takeaway: The non-inferiority margin must be set in advance.

questions.p:
Janice, 32, has been a strict vegan for 7 years and takes no supplements. Over 6 months she has had fatigue, poor concentration, irritability and tingling in both feet. On exam she has a smooth red tongue and reduced vibration and position sense in her toes.

Hb 88 g/L (ref 115-160)
MCV 118 fL (ref 80-100)
Reticulocytes low
WBC 3.6 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 128 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Methylmalonic acid high
Homocysteine high
Film: oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. A strict vegan diet, neurological signs with loss of proprioception, megaloblastic changes, and a high MMA plus homocysteine fit B12 deficiency. Body stores last 3 to 4 years, so it appears after years of a vegan diet.
A: Liver disease is non-megaloblastic.
B: Hypothyroidism is non-megaloblastic, with large round red cells and normal neutrophils.
C: Folate deficiency raises homocysteine only, and does not cause the neurological signs.
D: MDS is seen mostly in the elderly and would not explain a high MMA.
Takeaway: B12 stores last 3 to 4 years. Folate stores last 3 to 6 months.

questions.p:
Elsie, 71, recovered from a Mycoplasma pneumonia 3 weeks ago. Since then she has felt tired, and her fingers turn painful and pale when she goes outside in the cold. On exam she is pale with mild jaundice. Her spleen is not enlarged.

Hb 92 g/L (ref 115-160)
MCV 112 fL (ref 80-100)
Reticulocytes high
WBC 7.4 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 245 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
LDH high
Haptoglobin low
DAT positive for C3
Film: red cells clustered together in large groups.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: C. Agglutination, a DAT positive for C3, and symptoms in the cold after Mycoplasma infection fit cold AIHA. IgM antibodies bind at 4 to 30°C and form tetramers that link red cells.
A: Warm AIHA is IgG on the DAT and shows spherocytes without agglutination.
B: B12 deficiency is megaloblastic with a low reticulocyte count and no hemolysis on the DAT.
D: Myeloma causes rouleaux, a stack of coins, not clumps.
E: PNH is a clonal PIGA disorder and is not immune mediated.
Takeaway: Cold agglutinin disease can raise the MCV falsely, as clumps are counted as large cells.

questions.p:
A classmate thinks your patient's megaloblastic anemia is from folate deficiency. Which findings point to B12 deficiency instead?
i) A raised methylmalonic acid
ii) Loss of proprioception in the feet
iii) A raised homocysteine
iv) Hypersegmented neutrophils on the film
questions.e:
Correct: A. Methylmalonic acid rises only when B12 is low, and loss of proprioception is a B12 neurological feature.
B: Homocysteine rises in both deficiencies, so it does not separate them.
C: Homocysteine and hypersegmented neutrophils are shared by both.
D: Statements iii) and iv) occur in both deficiencies.
Takeaway: MMA plus homocysteine means B12. Homocysteine only means folate.

questions.p:
Leila, 38, has 1 week of fatigue, gum bleeding and large bruises. Today she has a headache. On exam she has petechiae, oozing gums and no lymph nodes or spleen.

Hb 86 g/L (ref 115-160)
WBC 1.8 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 22 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
PT/INR 1.8
Fibrinogen 0.9 g/L
D-dimer elevated
Film: abnormal promyelocytes, several with multiple Auer rods in the same cell.
Flow cytometry: HLA-DR negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. Pancytopenia with DIC, cells with 2 or more Auer rods, and HLA-DR negative flow fit APL. Its main early risk is fatal hemorrhage, often cerebral.
A: CML gives a high WBC with basophils, eosinophils and myelocytes.
B: ALL blasts have no granules and no Auer rods.
C: ITP lowers platelets only, with normal clotting tests.
D: Aplastic anemia has no abnormal cells in the blood and no DIC.
Takeaway: Confirm with t(15;17) or PML/RARα, and start ATRA.

questions.p:
Bruno, 58, has 3 months of fatigue, night sweats, weight loss and a heavy feeling in his left upper abdomen. On exam his spleen is palpable 10 cm below the costal margin. He has no lymph nodes.

Hb 112 g/L (ref 135-170)
WBC 180 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Basophils increased
Eosinophils increased
Platelets 560 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Film: myelocytes and neutrophils in a bimodal spread, with few blasts.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: C. A very high WBC with basophilia, eosinophilia, thrombocytosis, a bimodal spread of myelocytes and neutrophils, and a large spleen fit CML in chronic phase.
A: AML shows large blast cells, often with an Auer rod.
B: CLL raises mature lymphocytes, with smudge cells.
D: A reactive neutrophilia has no basophilia and shows toxic granules.
E: Myelofibrosis gives pancytopenia with teardrop cells.
Takeaway: Confirm with t(9;22) or BCR-ABL, and treat with imatinib.

questions.p:
Amira, 52, is in the ICU with septic shock from a perforated bowel. Over the last day she has started oozing from her IV and arterial line sites and has new purpura on her arms. She is on no anticoagulants.

Hb 84 g/L (ref 115-160)
WBC 21.0 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 35 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
PT/INR 2.0
aPTT prolonged
Fibrinogen 0.8 g/L
D-dimer markedly elevated
Film: schistocytes.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: D. Sepsis with bleeding, low platelets, a high INR, a fibrinogen under 1 g/L, a raised D-dimer and schistocytes fit DIC. Overactive coagulation consumes clotting factors and platelets.
A: TTP has a normal INR and fibrinogen.
B: ITP leaves the INR and fibrinogen normal.
C: HIT causes thrombosis without bleeding, after heparin exposure.
E: Vitamin K deficiency does not lower fibrinogen or platelets.
Takeaway: DIC bleeding: cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen is under 1.0 g/L, platelets if under 50, plasma if INR over 1.5.

questions.p: A patient on warfarin has a major GI bleed with a high INR. Which treatment reverses the warfarin?
questions.e:
Correct: B. Warfarin is reversed urgently with PCC. Vitamin K is given with it to prevent rebound coagulopathy when the PCC wears off.
A: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran.
C: Andexanet alpha is for Xa inhibitors and is pending approval.
D: Protamine reverses heparin.
E: DDAVP treats mild hemophilia A and type 1 VWD, and cryoprecipitate replaces fibrinogen.
Takeaway: Warfarin reversal: PCC plus vitamin K.

questions.p: Adam, 30, has an anterior mediastinal mass that has caused symptoms over several months. AFP is normal and beta-hCG is mildly raised. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.e:
Correct: B. An onset over months fits lymphoma or seminoma, and beta-hCG is raised in 10% of seminomas. AFP is the marker of non-seminomatous tumours.
A: Non-seminomatous tumours raise AFP in 60 to 80% and come on over days.
C: Lymphoblastic lymphoma comes on over days.
D: Thymoma grows over years and is linked to anti-AChR.
Takeaway: Days: lymphoblastic or NSGCT. Months: lymphoma, seminoma. Years: thymoma, teratoma.

questions.p:
Gloria, 70, has 3 days of fever, productive cough and right-sided chest pain. Chest X-ray shows a right lower lobe consolidation. She has no weight loss, night sweats or enlarged organs.

Hb 128 g/L (ref 115-160)
WBC 24 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Neutrophils 21, mature with some bands × 10⁹/L
Basophils normal
Platelets 380 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Film: toxic granules, toxic vacuoles and Döhle bodies. No blasts or promyelocytes.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: A. Mature neutrophils with toxic granules, toxic vacuoles and Döhle bodies, no blasts, and an obvious pneumonia fit a secondary, reactive neutrophilia.
B: CML shows basophilia, eosinophilia and myelocytes, usually with a large spleen.
C: CLL raises lymphocytes, not neutrophils.
D: AML shows blasts in the blood.
E: PV raises the Hb.
Takeaway: Primary neutrophilia: immature myeloid cells and often a WBC over 30.

questions.p: A 10-day-old boy has oozing from his umbilical stump and bleeds for days after circumcision. Platelets, INR, aPTT and fibrinogen are all normal. Which test should come next?
questions.e:
Correct: C. Bleeding with a normal INR and aPTT has a short list that includes FXIII deficiency, as in your Week 10 quiz. A factor XIII assay is one of the follow-up tests.
A: Anti-Xa measures the activity of heparin and Xa inhibitors.
B: A mixing study works up a prolonged clotting time, and his are normal.
D: D-dimers come from plasmin breaking down cross-linked fibrin and do not diagnose a factor deficiency.
Takeaway: Normal INR and PTT with bleeding: platelets, VWD, FXIII, fibrinolysis, vessels.

questions.p:
Albert, 79, has lower-risk MDS on IPSS. Which belong in his management?
i) Red cell transfusion when Hb falls below 70 g/L
ii) Growth factor support with EPO or G-CSF
iii) Monitoring and treating iron overload
iv) Hypomethylating agents to slow progression
questions.e:
Correct: A. Lower-risk MDS care aims at quality of life: transfusions below 70 g/L, managing iron overload and growth factor support.
B: This leaves out iron overload, which transfused patients need watched.
C: Hypomethylating agents such as azacitidine belong to higher-risk care.
D: Statement iv) is higher-risk management.
Takeaway: Lower risk: support. Higher risk: change the course.

questions.p:
Walter, 81, has eaten very little for 6 weeks since a stroke and has had courses of antibiotics for aspiration pneumonia. He now has easy bruising and blood in his urine. He takes no anticoagulants. His albumin and liver enzymes are normal.

Hb 124 g/L (ref 135-170)
Platelets 230 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
PT/INR 3.1
aPTT mildly prolonged
Fibrinogen normal

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. Poor intake with a high INR, a normal platelet count, a normal fibrinogen and normal liver tests fit vitamin K deficiency, which lowers factors II, VII, IX and X.
A: DIC lowers platelets and fibrinogen.
B: Hemophilia A prolongs the aPTT with a normal INR.
C: ITP gives a low platelet count with normal clotting tests.
D: VWD leaves the INR normal.
Takeaway: Severe liver disease can look similar, but it brings abnormal liver tests.

questions.p: A deficiency of which factor can greatly prolong the aPTT without causing bleeding?
questions.e:
Correct: D. Contact factors, including factor XII, can profoundly raise the aPTT but do not cause a bleeding tendency.
A: Factor IX deficiency is hemophilia B and causes bleeding.
B: Factor VIII deficiency is hemophilia A and causes bleeding.
C: Factor XI deficiency causes bleeding.
Takeaway: Factor XII is not required for clotting in the body.

questions.p: A 70-year-old man has a marrow core biopsy for anemia. Cellularity is reported as 30%. How is this best described?
o: Not assessable on a core biopsy
questions.e:
Correct: C. Marrow cellularity is about 100 minus age, so a 70-year-old should be about 30%.
A: Hypercellular is well above that, such as 80% in an 80-year-old in your Jeopardy deck.
B: Hypocellular is well below that, as in aplastic anemia.
D: Cellularity is assessed on the core biopsy.
Takeaway: Cellularity = 100 minus age.

questions.p: A deficiency of which clotting factor prolongs the PT/INR but leaves the aPTT normal?
questions.e:
Correct: E. An isolated high PT/INR points to the extrinsic pathway, which is factor VII.
A: Factor IX deficiency prolongs the aPTT.
B: Factor VIII deficiency prolongs the aPTT.
C: Factor XIII deficiency leaves both the INR and aPTT normal.
D: Factor XII deficiency prolongs the aPTT.
Takeaway: aPTT alone: VIII, IX, XI, XII. INR alone: VII. Both: X, V, II.

questions.p: Mia, 26, had radiation to her neck and mediastinum for Hodgkin lymphoma 3 months ago. When she bends her neck forward, she feels electric tingling down her arms and legs. Which explanation fits?
o: Radiation pericarditis, inflaming the heart sac
Transient demyelination of the spinal cord
questions.e:
Correct: D. Paresthesia into the arms and legs on neck flexion is L'Hermitte's sign, a subacute effect from transient demyelination of the spinal cord.
A: Hypothyroidism is a late effect and does not cause tingling on neck flexion.
B: Pericarditis is inflammation of the sac around the heart.
C: Pneumonitis causes fever, cough and dyspnea 6 to 12 weeks after mediastinal RT.
Takeaway: Subacute: pneumonitis, pericarditis, L'Hermitte's sign. Late: hypothyroidism, infertility, second cancers.

questions.p: Which of the following is associated with basophilic stippling on the blood film?
questions.e:
Correct: B. Basophilic stippling is a feature of sideroblastic anemia, and lead poisoning is a listed cause of sideroblastic anemia.
A: Anemia of chronic inflammation shows hypochromic cells without stippling.
C: Hereditary spherocytosis shows spherocytes.
D: Iron deficiency shows hypochromia, anisocytosis, target cells and elliptocytes.
Takeaway: TAILS: thalassemia, chronic inflammation, iron deficiency, lead, sideroblastic.
